stations.title: The pay survey
stations.where: McKinsey & Company, hired by General Motors
stations.what: A multi-industry study of executive pay, published in Harvard Business Review.
stations.pitch: From 1939 to 1950 hourly pay more than doubled while top management pay rose only 35 percent. Adjusted for inflation, executives were going backwards.
stations.spread: HBR made it an annual feature for more than a decade before it moved to McKinsey Quarterly. For several years Patton accounted for close to a tenth of McKinsey's billings. Duff McDonald calls this the original sin of executive pay.

stations.title: Pay becomes a field
stations.what: Executive compensation turns into a regular beat, led by Patton's annual reports.
stations.pitch: Pay is something you measure against other companies, not a moral question.
stations.spread: From 1948 to 1951 HBR ran about one pay article a year. A few years later it ran about five. Patton kept writing there for decades, from “What Is an Executive Worth?” (1961) to “Executive Compensation by 1970” (1964).

stations.title: Profit is the only job
stations.where: University of Chicago, writing in The New York Times Magazine
stations.what: The essay “The Social Responsibility of Business Is to Increase Its Profits.”
stations.pitch: A corporate manager works for the shareholders. Spending their money on anything else is taking it from them.
stations.spread: Friedman said what managers should do. He did not say how to make them do it. Two Chicago-trained economists in Rochester picked up that question.

stations.title: Agency theory
stations.where: University of Rochester, published in the Journal of Financial Economics
stations.what: “Theory of the Firm: Managerial Behavior, Agency Costs and Ownership Structure.”
stations.pitch: Managers are agents who will serve themselves unless their wealth rises and falls with the shareholders'. The fix is to pay them like owners.
stations.spread: They set out to turn Friedman's essay into the math of economics. It became the most cited paper in financial economics and the default lens of business schools.

stations.title: The buyback door opens
stations.where: Chairman of the SEC, appointed by Reagan from E.F. Hutton
stations.what: Rule 10b-18 gives companies a safe harbor from manipulation charges when they buy back their own stock.
stations.pitch: A company buying its own shares on the open market is not rigging its price.
stations.spread: Buybacks lift earnings per share and stock price, the exact numbers executive pay was being tied to. Two days after the rule passed, Jensen and Eugene Fama presented their agency papers at the Hoover Institution.

stations.title: It's not how much, but how
stations.who: Michael Jensen and Kevin J. Murphy
stations.where: Harvard Business School and the University of Rochester, in HBR May–June 1990
stations.what: “CEO Incentives: It's Not How Much You Pay, But How.”
stations.pitch: Corporate America, they wrote, “pays its most important leaders like bureaucrats.” Pay should swing hard with the stock price.
stations.spread: The idea left the journals and entered the boardroom. The Conference Board credits the article with the explosion in stock option grants that followed.

stations.title: Everyone can see everyone
stations.what: Companies must report top executive pay in clear, comparable tables.
stations.pitch: Sunlight will shame boards into restraint.
stations.spread: It armed the opposite instinct. Every board and consultant could now see what rival CEOs got, and nobody wanted a below-average CEO.

stations.title: The million dollar loophole
stations.what: Companies can no longer deduct salary above $1 million for top executives, unless the pay is performance based.
stations.pitch: A cap to rein in CEO pay.
stations.spread: Stock options counted as performance based, so pay moved into options. Companies below $1 million raised salaries to exactly $1 million. SEC chair Christopher Cox later said it earned a place in the Museum of Unintended Consequences.

stations.title: The Lake Wobegon machine
stations.who: Compensation consultants and board pay committees
stations.what: Boards set CEO pay by targeting the 50th or 75th percentile of a hand-picked peer group.
stations.pitch: We have to pay the market rate to keep talent.
stations.spread: If every board pays above the median, the median keeps rising. Median CEO pay went from $2.3 million in 1992 to $7.2 million in 2001. By 2000 stock options were 49 percent of S&P 500 CEO pay.

stations.title: The authors flinch
stations.who: Michael Jensen and Kevin J. Murphy
stations.where: Later papers and an unfinished book, CEO Pay and What to Do About It
stations.what: A reassessment of what their 1990 idea had become.
stations.pitch: Options were supposed to replace other pay, not sit on top of it.
stations.spread: Murphy said companies layered options onto already competitive packages, to their chagrin. Options had tripled inflation-adjusted S&P 500 CEO pay in under a decade. Murphy and Jensen blame Congress more than themselves.

stations.title: Where it landed
stations.what: CEO pay up 1,316 percent since 1978. Typical worker pay up 28 percent.
stations.spread: The ratio peaked at 408 to 1 in 2021 and was 325 to 1 in 2025. The 1993 loophole was repealed in 2017. Pay did not come back down, because the peer machine no longer needed it.

title: CEO pay
question: Why do CEOs make 325 times what a typical worker makes?

counterpoints.claim: CEO pay tracks the growth in company size, not just ideas or loopholes.
counterpoints.who: Xavier Gabaix and Augustin Landier, "Why Has CEO Pay Increased So Much?" (2008)

counterpoints.claim: Pay for top earners in other fields (lawyers, hedge funds, athletes) rose just as fast, so it may be a superstar economy, not a boardroom con.
Jensen and Murphy argued the option explosion came mostly from Congress (162(m)), not their paper.

open_questions: Did the 1991 SEC Section 16 change (exercise and sell options immediately) matter? Lazonick says yes.
Who were the named pay consultants of the 1990s (Towers Perrin, Pearl Meyer, Frederic W. Cook) and which CEOs set the leapfrog packages?
Graef Crystal, ex-consultant turned critic, In Search of Excess (1991): add as the whistleblower node.
Who funded the Rochester and Chicago work (foundations, think tanks)? Do not guess; source it.
Jack Welch 1981 Pierre Hotel speech as the CEO-side salesman of shareholder value.
intro: In 1965 a big-company CEO made about 21 times what a typical worker made. In 2025 it was 325 times. A consultant, two economists, a magazine, a regulator and a president each carried the idea one step further. Move the idea through the people who carried it.

Before that EPI relies on an older survey, and years that fall on a straight line between survey years are drawn hollow as estimates.

findings.title: The money came late
findings.text: The ratio barely moved from 1965 to 1973, hovering around 23 to 1. The ideas were born in the 1950s and 1970s. The money arrived later: a slow climb in the 1980s, then a near vertical jump in the 1990s.

findings.title: The pitch never changed
findings.text: Patton in 1951 and Jensen and Murphy in 1990 made the same sale: executives are underpaid compared with what they are worth. Only the justification changed, from fairness to incentives.

findings.title: Even its authors flinched
findings.text: Jensen and Murphy wanted options to replace other pay. Boards stacked options on top of pay they already gave. Murphy said it happened to their chagrin.
